```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

Two designs identify effects from timing and thresholds rather than from
measuring every confounder: units that adopt a treatment at different times, and
units just either side of a cutoff. `dmlrs` fits both with cross-fitted machine
learning for the nuisance functions.

```{r}
library(dmlrs)
```

## Staggered adoption

Units start treatment in different periods and some never do. Comparing early
and late adopters with one two-way fixed effects regression can give misleading
answers when effects change over time, so `dml_staggered_did()` follows Callaway
and Sant'Anna (2021). It estimates one effect \(ATT(g, t)\) for each cohort
\(g\) (units first treated in period \(g\)) and period \(t\), each from a clean
comparison group.

The simulated panel below has two cohorts and a never-treated group. Treatment
effects grow with time since adoption, and adoption depends on a covariate that
also shifts the outcome trend, so a plain difference in differences is biased.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
covariate <- rnorm(n)
cohort <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(covariate), sample(c(3, 4), n, replace = TRUE), NA)

panel <- expand.grid(id = seq_len(n), t = 1:6)
panel$g <- cohort[panel$id]
panel$x <- covariate[panel$id]
since <- ifelse(is.na(panel$g), -1, panel$t - panel$g)
effect <- ifelse(since >= 0, 1 + 0.5 * since, 0)
panel$y <- panel$x + (0.5 + 0.3 * panel$x) * panel$t + effect + rnorm(nrow(panel))
```

The data is long: one row per unit and period. `g` is the first treated period,
and `NA` or `Inf` marks never-treated units.

```{r}
fit <- dml_staggered_did(panel$y, panel["x"], panel$id, panel$t, panel$g,
                         ml_g = lrn_ols(), ml_m = lrn_logistic(),
                         control_group = "never_treated")
fit
```

Each row is named `ATT(g, pre, t)`. Pre-treatment rows are placebo checks and
should be close to zero. `plot()` shows one panel per cohort, with placebo
estimates in orange.

```{r, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

There are many group-time effects, so summarise them with `aggregate()`. An
event study lines the cohorts up by time since treatment, and the true effect is
\(1 + 0.5 \times\) that time.

```{r}
event_study <- aggregate(fit, "eventstudy")
event_study
plot(event_study)
```

`aggregate()` also works by `"group"` and `"time"`. Each result holds two fits,
`effects` and `overall`, so the usual methods apply:

```{r}
confint(aggregate(fit, "group")$overall)
```

When units share shocks, pass `cluster`. Standard errors and aggregations become
cluster-robust and whole clusters go to folds. Repeated cross-sections use
`panel = FALSE`.

## Regression discontinuity

In a regression discontinuity design, treatment switches on when a running
variable crosses a cutoff. Units just below and just above the cutoff are
comparable, so the jump in the outcome is the effect at the cutoff.

Covariates are not needed for identification, but they can make the estimate
more precise. `dml_rdflex()` adjusts the outcome with a cross-fitted prediction
from the covariates (Noack, Olma and Rothe, 2024), then runs a port of
`rdrobust` on the adjusted outcome.

```{r}
set.seed(7)
n <- 2000
score <- runif(n, -1, 1)
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * 4), n)
treated <- as.numeric(score >= 0)
y <- 0.5 * treated + score + 2 * x[, 1] + rnorm(n)

fit <- dml_rdflex(y, treated, x, score, ml_g = lrn_lasso_cv())
fit
confint(fit, "Robust")
```

The three rows are the conventional, bias-corrected and robust estimates. Report
the robust row: its interval accounts for the bias of the local polynomial, and
the conventional one does not.

To see what the covariates add, compare with an estimate that ignores them:

```{r}
without <- dml_rdflex(y, treated, matrix(rnorm(n * 2), n), score, ml_g = lrn_ols())
c(without = unname(without$se["Robust"]), with = unname(fit$se["Robust"]))
```

In a fuzzy design the cutoff only changes the chance of treatment. Pass the
treatment received, a classifier and `fuzzy = TRUE`. The options of
`rdrobust::rdrobust()` go through `...`, for example `vce = "hc1"` or
`bwselect = "msetwo"`, and `cluster` gives cluster-robust standard errors.

```{r}
received <- rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(score >= 0, 0.8, 0.2))
y_fuzzy <- 0.5 * received + score + 2 * x[, 1] + rnorm(n)
dml_rdflex(y_fuzzy, received, x, score, ml_g = lrn_lasso_cv(),
           ml_m = lrn_logistic_cv(), fuzzy = TRUE)
```

## References

Callaway, B. and Sant'Anna, P. H. C. (2021). Difference-in-differences with
multiple time periods. *Journal of Econometrics*, 225(2), 200-230.

Noack, C., Olma, T. and Rothe, C. (2024). Flexible covariate adjustments in
regression discontinuity designs. arXiv:2107.07942.
